opus-5.5.text:
Well, it actually took us a while to really get it. When we released Fawkes back in 2020, we got a lot of email from all kinds of people, and among them was a steady trickle from artists asking, "Can I use this on my artwork?" Honestly, at the time we didn't fully understand the question. Fawkes was designed around facial recognition: it perturbs your photos so a model learns the wrong features for your face. Art didn't seem like the same problem, so we'd politely say it wasn't really built for that.

Then in 2022 everything changed with the explosion of text-to-image diffusion models: Stable Diffusion, Midjourney, and so on. Suddenly it became very clear what the artists had been worried about. These models were trained on huge scrapes of the internet, including artists' portfolios, and people were fine-tuning models on a specific artist's work to mimic their style and churning out imitations, sometimes with the artist's name attached.

The real turning point for me was when we got invited to an online town hall organized by artists, I believe late 2022. Hundreds of artists were on, talking about what this was doing to them: lost commissions, students questioning whether to pursue art at all, people seeing their life's work, their identity really, being absorbed and reproduced without consent or compensation. Hearing that firsthand was eye-opening. It wasn't an abstract privacy issue; it was people's livelihoods and their sense of self.

So we came back and said, okay, we have some expertise in adversarial perturbations against models. Can we do for artistic style what Fawkes did for faces? That became the starting point for Glaze. Style is a much harder, fuzzier target than a face, and the models are very different, so it was a substantial research effort. But the motivation came directly from listening to the artists and finally understanding what they had been asking us all along.

r001.rationale: The response connects artists’ questions about Fawkes to their work being included in large-scale training data and used to fine-tune generative image models.

r002.rationale: It says people fine-tuned models on a specific artist’s work to mimic their style, sometimes with the artist’s name attached.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this was a surprise to us, honestly. Fawkes was a project that we'd released in the summer of 2020, and it was very much aimed at people—at individuals—who were worried about their photos being scraped off social media and fed into these facial recognition models, things like Clearview AI. So the mental model we had was, you know, you're a person, you post selfies, you want to make sure that those selfies can't be used to train a model that recognizes your face. That's it. That was the whole scope.

And then in the fall of 2022, right around when the big text-to-image models really hit—Stable Diffusion had just come out, Midjourney was gaining a lot of traction—we started getting these emails. And they were from artists. And they were all asking some version of the same question, which was, "Can Fawkes protect my art?" And at first I didn't really understand the question. I remember thinking, well, no, it's a face tool, it only works on faces, what are you talking about? There's no face in a landscape painting.

But they kept coming. And so at some point I actually sat down and started reading what they were saying, and then I got on calls with a few of them. And what became clear pretty quickly was that they weren't confused about what Fawkes did. They understood it was for faces. What they were really asking was, is there anything like this for us? Because they had figured out, well before most of the ML community was willing to talk about it, that these models were being trained on their work. People were typing their names into prompts and getting out images that looked like their style, their portfolio, work that had taken them decades to develop. And they were watching their commissions disappear in real time.

So the question "can Fawkes protect my art" was really a question of, here's a group of people who built a tool that makes images useless for training a model. We're people whose images are being used to train a model without our consent. Can you help us? And once I understood it that way, it was kind of obvious that we had to at least try. That's where Glaze came from. We talked to a lot of artists—Karla Ortiz was one of the first, and then many others—and we spent a lot of time just listening before we wrote any code, because the threat model and what artists actually cared about were pretty different from what we'd assumed going in.

r001.rationale: The response says artists realized generative image models were being trained on their work and asked whether Fawkes could help protect it.

r002.rationale: It says people prompted models with artists’ names and received images resembling their style and portfolio.

astra-6.text:
At first, we didn’t really understand the connection. Fawkes was designed to protect people’s faces from facial recognition, so why were artists asking us about it? As we talked with them, we began to understand that they were worried about a similar loss of control: their work could be collected and used to train a model without their permission.

For an artist, a style can represent years of practice and experimentation. The concern wasn’t simply that someone could copy one image. It was that a model could learn to imitate that style and generate new work that could compete with them. That helped us understand why they were reaching out. They were asking whether the idea behind Fawkes—changing what a model learns from an image—could help them protect their work, too.

r001.rationale: It says artists feared their work could be collected and used to train a model without permission, connecting their inquiries to model training.

r002.rationale: It says a model could imitate an artist’s style, but does not explain that people could use the artist’s name as a prompt.

sol-6.1.text: At first, we didn’t understand the connection. Fawkes was designed to protect people’s faces from being used to train facial recognition systems, so why were artists asking us about their artwork? As we talked with them, we realized they were worried about something very similar: their work was being collected without their permission to train models that could imitate their style. For an artist, that style isn’t just a visual characteristic. It’s something they’ve spent years developing, and it’s tied to their identity and their livelihood. That helped us understand why they saw Fawkes as potentially relevant, even though protecting an artistic style turned out to be a very different technical problem from protecting a face.

r001.rationale: The response says artists feared their work was collected without permission to train models that could imitate their style.

r002.rationale: It mentions style imitation but does not explain that users could prompt a model with an artist’s name to produce it.
